SocialAgent Workshop

ODD+LLM: Specifying LLM-Agent Behavior
for Reproducible Social Simulation

Justin Downes Affiliation: Amazon Web Services Email: jusdow@amazon.com    Robby Milletich Affiliation: Amazon Web Services Email: rmilleti@amazon.com    Newel Hirst Affiliation: Amazon Web Services Email: nhirst@amazon.com
Abstract

The ODD protocol is the de facto standard for describing agent-based models, but it lacks vocabulary for the components that determine LLM-agent behavior: prompt assembly, memory serialization, parsing, and retry logic. We propose ODD+LLM, a backward-compatible extension adding five documentation blocks grounded in the CoALA cognitive-architecture framework. To show that the gap matters, we conduct a multiverse analysis (Steegen et al., 2016) of a published LLM naming-game simulation, varying six specification choices a reimplementer must make. Variants that are defensible readings of the paper stay within statistical noise of our baseline reconstruction. Missing one instruction that the paper states but is easy to overlook (that the model answers as an outside observer rather than as a player) raises the share of runs settling on the convention agents individually favor from 0.35 to 1.00 and makes convergence three times faster, in a reimplementation that uses a different model from the original. We complement the demonstration with a reconstruction-sufficiency review of 28 published LLM-agent simulations, finding that the details of how prompts are built and how model outputs are parsed are undetermined in 77% of cases, and that no paper fully specifies its main LLM call. ODD+LLM gives the field a standard home for information it already produces but currently scatters across code repositories, supplementary files, and undocumented defaults.

1 Introduction

The ODD protocol (Grimm et al., 2006; Grimm et al., 2010; Grimm et al., 2020) standardized agent-based model description by providing a structured template complete enough that an independent modeler can reimplement a model and recover its results. Its core is the Submodels block, where agent behavior is specified as equations or rules; the other blocks describe the model around it.

LLM-agent simulations have no Submodels block, and no vocabulary for writing one. ODD is already being adopted for this purpose; YuLan-OneSim (Wang et al., 2025b) generates executable simulators from LLM-authored ODD protocols across fifty social-science scenarios, but the protocols it produces specify agent types and interaction patterns while saying nothing about how context is assembled or how output becomes an action. An LLM agent’s action is the output of a sampling procedure applied to a token sequence assembled at runtime from a system prompt, a persona, some subset of interaction history, some rendering of environment state, and an output instruction, then parsed, possibly rejected, possibly resampled, and mapped onto a simulation action. That assembly procedure is what a Submodels block for LLM agents must describe.

This matters in practice. Ye et al. (2026) hold persona content fixed and vary only its presentation (prose, bullet list, key–value table), observing a 76-percentage-point difference in cooperation rate (N=30N{=}30 seeds, p<0.001p{<}0.001). Two papers reporting “agents were given demographic personas” can therefore support opposite conclusions about whether LLM agents cooperate.

ODD+LLM is a reporting standard, not a new algorithm. Like ODD itself and reporting guidelines such as CONSORT (Schulz et al., 2010) and TRIPOD (Collins et al., 2015), its contribution is what it standardizes and the evidence that those items matter. We make three contributions:

  1. 1.

    ODD+LLM: a backward-compatible extension to ODD adding five documentation blocks for LLM-agent simulations (§3). Blocks C and D use repeated records (one per model role and one per call site), following ODD’s existing pattern for submodels. The core of the protocol is Block D, the behavioral submodel, which specifies each LLM call in the loop by signature, binding, and resolution.

  2. 2.

    A multiverse demonstration that specification salience is consequential (§4). We take a published naming-game simulation (Flint Ashery et al., 2025a), identify six specification choices (four from supplementary materials, one in main text but non-obvious, one genuinely open), implement a baseline and seven one-factor variants, and show that missing a single stated but easily overlooked instruction determines the headline result.

  3. 3.

    A reconstruction-sufficiency review of 28 LLM-agent simulations coded for where an independent implementer would have to guess (§5).

2 Related Work

ODD and its extensions.

ODD (Grimm et al., 2006; Grimm et al., 2010) was extended to ODD+D for decision-making (Müller et al., 2013), ODD+2D for data-driven models (Laatabi et al., 2018), vODD-DD for visual documentation (Lee and Lazarova-Molnar, 2026), and VISA for machine-reproducible descriptions (He, 2026). None address the prompt-assembly problem because it did not exist before LLM agents. The closest antecedent is the move from verbal rules to equations in ODD 2020 (Grimm et al., 2020), which argued that natural-language descriptions of behavior are insufficient for reconstruction, precisely the claim we make about LLM-agent descriptions. VISA opens with nearly our framing (“two readers routinely reconstruct different models from the same documentation”) but targets classical ABMs rather than LLM-agent behavior.

ODD applied to LLM-agent simulation.

YuLan-OneSim (Wang et al., 2025b) generates executable LLM-agent simulators from ODD protocols across 50 social-science scenarios. They use ODD forward (natural language →\to ODD →\to code), whereas we test it backward (published study →\to could an implementer reconstruct it?). Their generated protocols specify agent types and interaction patterns but contain nothing about which model runs, how context is assembled, or how output is parsed; those choices are resolved downstream by code templates and configuration. A system that already wants ODD for LLM agents is evidence of demand; that its protocols stop where Blocks C and D begin is evidence of the gap.

Validity critiques of LLM-agent simulations.

Larooij and Törnberg (2025) review 35 papers and find systematic validation gaps. Zhou et al. (2025) propose six design-validity principles (PIMMUR) and re-run five papers. Ye et al. (2026) demonstrate that format-only perturbations move outcomes by up to 76pp, though the same perturbation on deepseek-v3 produces ∼{\sim}1pp, indicating strong model-dependence. Barrie and Törnberg (2025) argue that naming-game results are observationally equivalent to data leakage from pretraining; Flint Ashery et al. (2025b) respond that the effect survives controls. Our work complements these critiques by providing a specification, and our multiverse analysis measures the range of outcomes consistent with a description rather than testing whether a specific mechanism is correct.

Representation-effect audits.

Ye et al. (2026)’s TRAILS-R taxonomy audits representation-level perturbations (formatting, delimiter choice, output schema, instruction order, memory representation) that map onto our Block D items DB-1 through DB-7. We adopt their three-level claim_strength hierarchy (exploratory, mechanism, policy) for our corpus metadata. TRAILS is an audit taxonomy (what to perturb to test robustness), while ODD+LLM is a documentation protocol (what to write down so a finding can be reconstructed at all). Block D’s resolution layer (parser, validity constraints, retry, failure cascade, failure rate) has no TRAILS analogue, and our reconstruction-sufficiency review measures determinability rather than robustness. TRAILS found that memory representation had the smallest effect among the representation axes they tested, independently corroborating our Stage 2 finding that memory-format and memory-order arms (M1, M2) produce small population-level effects relative to person framing (M4).

Cognitive-architecture frameworks.

CoALA (Sumers et al., 2024) provides a taxonomy of LLM-agent components (working memory, long-term memory, internal/external actions, decision procedure). We adopt it as the ontology for Block A rather than inventing one. DSPy (Khattab et al., 2024) provides a machine-readable signature format for LLM modules; Block D’s schema draws on it.

3 The ODD+LLM Protocol

ODD+LLM adds five blocks to the standard ODD template. The existing ODD blocks (Purpose, Entities/State Variables, Process Overview, Design Concepts, Initialization, Input Data, Submodels) are retained unchanged; the extension occupies a new section between Design Concepts and Initialization.

Following ODD’s own pattern (Submodels is already one entry per submodel; State Variables is a list), Blocks C and D are repeated records. Block C has one record per model role and Block D one per LLM call site, so documentation grows with the system. A two-agent dilemma with one call site stays a one-page specification, while a generative-architecture paper with nine distinct calls produces nine records.

3.1 Block A: Cognitive Architecture (CoALA-structured)

Documents the agent’s information-processing architecture using CoALA’s taxonomy (9 items): working memory contents per cycle; long-term memory types, backing store, retrieval rule (formula and cardinality), and write rule; internal and external action spaces; decision procedure (including actions per activation); tools; and the inter-agent communication channel with its visibility parameter.

3.2 Block B: Identity

Documents persona source, content, surface form (the verbatim template), heterogeneity method, behavioral constraints, and identity stability (static vs. drifting, with the update rule). The surface-form item is marked as behavioral rather than cosmetic, following Ye et al. (2026)’s finding. (6 items.)

3.3 Block C: Inference Configuration

Block C has a two-item spine at the system level and a per-role record (6 items) repeated for each model or API in the behavior or measurement path.

C-spine (system level).

  • •

    CS1: Known provider-side non-determinism sources (batching, routing, caching) and their handling.

  • •

    CS2: Execution concurrency and ordering: whether calls are issued sequentially, concurrently, or asynchronously, and whether intra-timestep ordering is deterministic.

C-role (repeated per model role).

Roles observed in the corpus include agent, classifier, judge, embedder, generator (offline content), and external API. Each record contains:

  • •

    CR1–CR3: Model identity (exact version string or pinned snapshot), build identity (system fingerprint), and provider/endpoint/API version/access date.

  • •

    CR4: Decoding parameters, named unambiguously and distinguished from same-named training or reward parameters.

  • •

    CR5: Serving precision and quantization.

  • •

    CR6: Training or adaptation (base checkpoint, method, data construction, objective, selection criterion). Marked NA if used off the shelf.

Every model role gets a record. An unnamed embedder is a role record scoring 0 on CR1, not a footnote.

3.4 Block D: Behavioral Submodel

Block D is the ODD Submodels equivalent for LLM agents. Like Block C, it has a two-item spine at the system level and a per-call-site record (15 items) repeated for each distinct LLM call in the simulation loop. Items within a call-site record are grouped into four sections:

D-spine (system level).

  • •

    DG1: Temporal coupling: whether step tt output enters step t+1t{+}1 input, and in what form.

  • •

    DG2: Scheduling and activation: timestep duration, who acts when, within-step ordering. Controlled vocabulary adopted from Concordia (Vezhnevets et al., 2023): simultaneous/sequential/asynchronous.

Signature (what the call is).

  • •

    DS-1: Input bindings: which state variables feed this call.

  • •

    DS-2: Output type or schema.

Binding (how it is rendered).

  • •

    DB-1: Static text (system prompt and fixed instructions, verbatim).

  • •

    DB-2: Serialization per slot: how each variable renders into text.

  • •

    DB-3: Component order and system-vs-user role placement.

  • •

    DB-4: History policy with cardinality (“top-ranked memories” without a kk is underdetermined).

  • •

    DB-5: Truncation/summarization rule with constants.

  • •

    DB-6: Token budget and drop order.

  • •

    DB-7: Action-space encoding: how the option set is presented.

Resolution (how output becomes an action).

  • •

    DR-1: Parser: exact extraction procedure.

  • •

    DR-2: Validity constraints: what makes a parseable output invalid.

  • •

    DR-3: Retry policy: count, whether prompt is modified, fallback on final failure.

  • •

    DR-4: Failure action and cascade: what the system does, and what other agents observe.

  • •

    DR-5: Failure rate (an empirical result, included to force reporting; analogous to ODD’s “Output Data”).

Delegation.

  • •

    DF-1: Third-party framework: library name, pinned version, and which part of assembly or resolution it owns. An unpinned framework dependency is undetermined.

Systems with multiple call sites.

Complex architectures may call the LLM in several places (e.g., acting, reflecting, summarizing memory). Document the primary call site, the one that produces the agent’s behavioral output, against all 15 items. List any other call sites in a short inventory that names each one and marks whether it is fully documented. A simple model stays at one record, and readers can still see how much of a complex architecture is specified.

Block D is designed so that a .yaml configuration file satisfying the schema is the Block D documentation; no separate prose description is needed. The arm configurations for our multiverse analysis (§4) are themselves Block D specifications.

3.5 Block E: Validation

Documents behavioral reference, validation level, replication count (E3a) and the unit over which variance is reported (E3b), variance reporting, representation sensitivity (whether any prompt-form perturbation was tested), population dispersion, ablation and non-social controls (E7a), non-LLM or human baselines (E7b), and longitudinal stability. (10 items.)

The E3 and E7 splits distinguish papers that state n=1n{=}1 from those that never state nn, and papers with ablation controls from those with human baselines, distinctions that collapsed in an earlier draft and obscured the dominant failure mode.

4 Multiverse Demonstration

We select Flint Ashery et al. (2025a), “Emergent social conventions and collective bias in LLM populations” (Science Advances, 2025). In this naming game, N=24N{=}24 agents repeatedly choose names from a pool of W=2W{=}2 letters; matching earns +100+100, mismatching costs −50-50. The paper reports that individually unbiased agents converge disproportionately to one “strong” convention, driven by microscopic asymmetry in stick-after-success vs. switch-after-failure behavior.

We chose this paper because it is well documented by current norms. It reports model versions, includes real controls, provides supplementary prompts, and publishes code (github.com/Ariel-Flint-Ashery/AI-norms). This makes it a conservative test case. The gaps we identify exist despite above-average documentation, because there is no standard home for the information Block D requires.

Branch points.

We identify six specification choices from the 21 decision points our instrument assigns to this paper, selected on the basis that each corresponds to a choice our rubric flags as behaviorally relevant (changes_behavior: certain or likely):

We implement eight arms: one baseline (our best reading of the main text) plus one alternative per branch point (with M1 having two alternatives). All arms share N=24N{=}24, W=2W{=}2, H=5H{=}5, payoffs +100/−50+100/-50, and chain-of-thought prompting, everything the paper does specify. We use Claude Sonnet 4.6 (via AWS Bedrock, temperature 0.7) rather than the paper’s original models (which specify temperature 0.5, top-k 10, max tokens 6 in Table S4 of the supplementary). Both deviations illustrate the specification-salience problem, because the original values are in the supplementary materials but are easy to miss.

Stage 1: Memory-state probe.

Before running full simulations, we synthesize memory states and query the model directly (7 states ×\times 8 arms ×\times 300 samples = 16,800 calls). This measures the microscopic asymmetry the paper identifies as the origin of collective bias.

Stage 2: Full simulation.

We run 20 seeds per arm (8 arms ×\times 20 seeds ×\times ∼\sim200 calls/seed ≈\approx 32,000 LLM calls). The headline metric is P⁡(M)P(M): the fraction of runs whose consensus convention is M.

Interpretation.

The specification curve (Simonsohn et al., 2020) (Figure 1) separates two kinds of arm. The six arms that vary a choice the main text leaves open or delegates to the supplement span P⁡(M)∈[0.30,0.55]P(M)\in[0.30,0.55], all within noise of the baseline. M4 is different in kind. It reverses an instruction the paper states, so it tests what happens when salient information is missed rather than offering a seventh defensible reconstruction. Two tensions constrain the claim.

Stage 1 vs. Stage 2. The microscopic probe (Table 2) shows M as the “strong” convention (baseline asymmetry +0.200+0.200), yet the population simulation lands on Q two-thirds of the time (P⁡(M)=0.350P(M){=}0.350). This reversal likely reflects stochastic dynamics at 20 seeds. Every third-person arm’s Wilson CI covers 0.5, so none can be distinguished from a fair coin. The detectable signal is M4 alone.

A single-item claim. We do not claim that six choices determine the outcome. Missing one stated instruction, person framing, changes it in our reimplementation (P⁡(M)=1.00P(M){=}1.00 in all 20 seeds, convergence three times faster; Figure 2), while five further choices plausibly modulate the outcome below our detection power. Because we also substitute the model and decoding settings, the result shows sensitivity in this reimplementation, not a property of the original system. It still matters in practice, because an implementer who writes first-person instructions (the natural default for “a naming-game simulation”) would observe a qualitatively different phenomenon.

Specification salience. M4 is specified in the paper (“external observer forecasting Player 1”) and is thus not underspecified in the strict sense. But it demonstrates that even specified information can fail to reach an independent reader if it has no standard home. Only M6 (parse failure) is genuinely open, and it returns the baseline P⁡(M)P(M) of 0.350 exactly. Parse failures occur in under 1% of calls, so the branch almost never fires, which shows where specification effort matters.

5 Reconstruction-Sufficiency Review

We code 28 published LLM-agent simulations (2023–2026) for reconstruction sufficiency, stratified by architecture: minimal-choice agents, opinion dynamics, platform-scale simulators, economic/market models, full generative architectures, policy testbeds, and norm emergence. For each paper, we ask one question per item: could an independent implementer, reading only this paper and its linked artifacts, determine this, or would they have to guess?

Instrument.

Items are scored 0 (undetermined), 1 (partially determined: the component is named but at least one behaviorally relevant aspect remains open), or 2 (determined). The key distinction is between asserting that a component exists and specifying it. “Agents have a memory module” asserts a component exists; it does not specify what enters it, how it is rendered, or when it is cleared. Assertion without operational content scores 1, never 2. Every score of 0 or 1 generates a named decision point, an independently variable choice that two implementers could set differently without contradicting the text.

The instrument was derived from 10 papers screened in Pass 1 (9 eligible, 1 excluded on read), during which the repeated-record structure emerged from corpus evidence then frozen as v1. Pass 2 codes the remaining 19 papers with the frozen instrument unchanged; decision points that do not fit the block structure are recorded as misses and reported.

Each paper carries a claim_strength label (exploratory, mechanism, or policy; following the TRAILS hierarchy (Ye et al., 2026)), letting us test whether the strongest empirical claims rest on the weakest specifications.

Results.

Of 32 papers screened, 4 were excluded on read (2×\timesE1, 1×\timesE3, 1 deferred), yielding 28 coded papers across 18 venues and 7 strata (2023–2026); all 28 are listed individually in Table 5. Because Blocks C and D are repeated records, papers have different denominators and raw item counts are not comparable. We therefore report three numbers.

(1) System-block coverage. The mean sufficiency score across the 29 system-level items is 1.52/2.00 (76%). Architecture (Block A: 1.63) and validation (Block E: 1.46) are documented reasonably well. Inference configuration is not. Block C averages 0.48/2.00 per role and 0.00 on system fingerprint (CR2), which scored 0 in all 28 papers.

(2) Fraction of papers whose primary call site is fully determined. None of the 28 primary call sites scored 2 on every binding and resolution item. The resolution layer (DR1–DR5) is nearly absent from the literature: 96% of resolution item-scores are <<2 (i.e., not fully determined); retry policy (DR3) scores 0 in 85% of papers; parse-failure rate (DR5) is unreported in 93%. Block D binding items (DB1–DB7) fare better at 1.14/2.00 but still leave 62% of item-scores at 0 or 1. The combined undetermination rate across binding and resolution items (fraction of item-scores <<2) is 77% (236/306).

(3) Complexity. Papers average 1.5 model roles (range 1–3); only the primary call site is formally coded. Block C averages 0.53/2.00 for agent roles alone but 0.48 across all roles, confirming that secondary models are systematically invisible.

Decision points.

The 28 papers yield 705 decision points (mean 25.2 per paper, range 10–40). The inventory saturated by paper 15: fewer than 2 novel axes per paper thereafter, suggesting that the block structure derived from Pass 1 generalizes to the held-out set. Zero decision points required a block the frozen instrument could not house.

Claim strength vs. specification.

Papers making mechanism claims (n=11n{=}11) average a per-paper Block D call-site score of 1.00/2.00; policy claims (n=9n{=}9) average 0.72. Stratum is a confounder (policy papers cluster in more complex architectures) and the difference is not statistically tested at this sample size.

6 Discussion

The protocol records choices already made.

Every Block D item corresponds to a choice the implementer has already made; the protocol asks only that it be written in a standard location. For our own study this took one configuration file plus a results section (DR-5, Block E; Appendix E). We have not measured author burden more generally. Our multiverse arm configurations are Block D specifications, and losing one stated item from them produced a qualitatively different outcome.

Limitations.

Demonstration. The multiverse is a single case study with 20 seeds per arm. It shows that one specification item can determine a result but does not estimate how often this happens across simulations. It uses one model (Claude Sonnet 4.6) with decoding settings that differ from the original, so magnitudes may differ with other models. The design is one-factor-at-a-time (8 arms), not a full factorial (26=642^{6}{=}64); interactions between axes are untested. With 20 seeds, only M4 is statistically separable; the remaining branches may modulate outcomes below our detection power. M4 is specified in the source paper (“external observer”), so first-person framing is a sensitivity test of what happens when salient-but-non-obvious information is missed, not a defensible reconstruction. Coverage of the protocol. The multiverse exercises six items (DB-1 to DB-4, DG2, DR-3). The remaining items are motivated by how often the corpus leaves them undetermined and by prior evidence such as Ye et al. (2026), not by experiment; validating each item is future work. Evidence for the standard. The rubric is new and was applied by a single coder without inter-rater reliability estimation, so the 77% figure is indicative rather than validated. We have not yet shown that ODD+LLM improves reconstruction or measured its cost to authors. Double-coding a subset of the corpus and a study in which readers reconstruct calls from completed specifications are the next steps. The current protocol assumes text-in/text-out calls; multimodal inputs (images, video frames) to vision-language models are not covered.

Not a critique.

Flint Ashery et al. is well-documented by current norms. The information exists; what is missing is salience, a standard place for choices that are already made.

Conclusion.

ODD+LLM gives the LLM-agent simulation community a structured home for specification decisions that determine behavior. It is a documentation convention that reduces avoidable ambiguity. It cannot guarantee reproducibility, because models change, providers update silently, and stochastic systems are inherently variable. But the choices a researcher can pin down should be pinned down. Missing one stated instruction flips a reimplementation’s headline result; 77% of binding and resolution items across 28 papers are undetermined. Adopting the protocol costs one configuration file; Figure 1 shows the cost of leaving these choices undocumented.

Appendix A Per-Paper Sufficiency Scores

Table 5 reports the sufficiency scores for all 28 coded papers. System mean is over the 29 system-level items (Blocks A, B, C-spine, D-spine, E). D-site mean is over the 15 per-call-site items for the primary call site. DPs is the count of decision points, independently variable choices the text leaves open.

Table 6 shows the score distribution for Block D call-site items across the 28 primary call sites. The resolution layer (DR1–DR5) is systematically absent.

Appendix C Corpus and Exclusions

The corpus was drawn from a pre-specified venue set (ACL, EMNLP, NAACL, COLING, NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, AAAI, IJCAI, AAMAS, ICWSM, WWW, CHI, JASSS, Science Advances, Nature Human Behaviour, PNAS, arXiv cs.MA/cs.CL/physics.soc-ph), 2023–2026.

Inclusion.

≥\geq1 LLM-driven agent whose behavior is repeatedly elicited over ≥\geq2 timesteps with state carried forward, interacting with at least one other party (LLM, scripted, or human), in a social, economic, or political scenario.

Flow.

48 records identified →\to 16 excluded at title/abstract screening →\to 32 screened on read →\to 4 excluded on read →\to 28 coded.

Exclusions on read.

horton2023 (E1: one-shot vignettes, no carried-forward state), park2024 (E1: independent questionnaire responses, no inter-agent interaction), abdelnabi2023 (E3: evaluation benchmark, not social simulation), relorder2026 (deferred: retrieval failure). Screening exclusions: 7×\timesE3 task-completion, 3×\timesE2 non-human actors, 3×\timesE4 methodology papers, 3×\timesE5 framework papers.

Appendix D Coding Instrument (v1)

The full instrument, frozen 2026-08-15 after Pass 1. Every item answers one question: Could an independent implementer, reading only this paper and its linked artifacts, determine this, or would they have to guess?

Score scale.

2 (Determined): an implementer could set this correctly without guessing. 1 (Partially determined): named with some content, but at least one behaviorally relevant aspect remains open; assertion without operational content scores 1, never 2. 0 (Undetermined): absent or constrains nothing. NA: the system genuinely has no such component. UNVERIFIED: artifact exists but coder could not obtain it; excluded from denominators.

Decision-point granularity.

One decision point = one independently variable choice that could be set differently without contradicting the text. This is deliberately the same definition as a multiverse branch point.

Block A: Cognitive Architecture (9 items).

  1. A1.

    Working memory contents per cycle

  2. A2.

    Long-term memory types and backing store

  3. A3.

    Retrieval rule (formula, constants, cardinality)

  4. A4.

    Learning/write rule

  5. A5.

    Internal action space

  6. A6.

    External action space

  7. A7.

    Decision procedure (incl. actions per activation)

  8. A8.

    Tools (or NA)

  9. A9.

    Inter-agent channel and visibility parameter

Block B: Identity (6 items).

  1. B1.

    Persona source

  2. B2.

    Persona content

  3. B3.

    Persona surface form (verbatim template)

  4. B4.

    Heterogeneity method

  5. B5.

    Behavioral constraints

  6. B6.

    Identity stability (static/drifting, with update rule)

Block C spine (2 items).

  1. CS1.

    Provider-side non-determinism sources and handling

  2. CS2.

    Execution concurrency and ordering

Block D spine (2 items).

  1. DG1.

    Temporal coupling (step tt output →\to step t+1t{+}1 input)

  2. DG2.

    Scheduling and activation (timestep, who acts, ordering)

Block E: Validation (10 items).

  1. E1.

    Behavioral reference

  2. E2.

    Validation level

  3. E3a.

    Replication count stated

  4. E3b.

    Variance unit

  5. E4.

    Variance reporting

  6. E5.

    Representation sensitivity

  7. E6.

    Population dispersion

  8. E7a.

    Ablation/non-social control

  9. E7b.

    Non-LLM or human baseline

  10. E8.

    Longitudinal stability

Per model role (6 items, repeated).

Roles: agent, classifier, judge, embedder, generator, external API.

  1. CR1.

    Model identity (exact version string)

  2. CR2.

    Build identity (system fingerprint)

  3. CR3.

    Provider, endpoint, API version, access date

  4. CR4.

    Decoding parameters (named unambiguously)

  5. CR5.

    Serving precision and quantization

  6. CR6.

    Training/adaptation (NA if off-the-shelf)

Per call site (15 items, repeated).

Signature:

  1. DS-1.

    Input bindings (which state variables feed this call)

  2. DS-2.

    Output type or schema

Binding:

  1. DB-1.

    Static text (system prompt, verbatim)

  2. DB-2.

    Serialization per slot

  3. DB-3.

    Component order and role placement

  4. DB-4.

    History policy with cardinality

  5. DB-5.

    Truncation/summarization rule with constants

  6. DB-6.

    Token budget and drop order

  7. DB-7.

    Action-space encoding

Resolution:

  1. DR-1.

    Parser (exact extraction procedure)

  2. DR-2.

    Validity constraints

  3. DR-3.

    Retry policy (count, prompt modification, fallback)

  4. DR-4.

    Failure action and cascade

  5. DR-5.

    Failure rate (reported as result)

Delegation:

  1. DF-1.

    Third-party framework (library, pinned version, scope)

Appendix E Worked Example: Block D for the Naming Game

Our multiverse arm configurations are themselves Block D specifications. Below we show how the baseline configuration (base.yaml) maps to each protocol item.

experiment:
  population_size: 24
  name_pool: ["M", "Q"]
  memory_length: 5
  payoff_success: 100
  payoff_failure: -50

model:
  provider: "bedrock"
  name: "us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6"
  temperature: 0.7
  top_k: 40
  max_tokens: 1024

branch:
  memory_format: "table"       # DB-2
  memory_order: "recent_first" # DB-3
  score_semantics: "window_sum"# DB-4
  person_framing: "third_person_observer" # DB-1
  pairing: "random_pair_per_step"         # DG2
  parse_failure: "resample_max_3"         # DR-3

fixed:
  randomize_name_order: true   # DB-7
  cot: true                    # DB-1

Item mapping.

DG1 (temporal coupling): step tt output (chosen name, payoff) enters step t+1t{+}1 as a memory row. DG2: random-pair-per-step, sequential within step. DS-1: f​(persona,memory​[H],score,name_pool)f(\text{persona},\text{memory}[H],\text{score},\text{name\_pool}). DS-2: single letter from name pool. DB-1: fixed system prompt with third-person observer framing and CoT instruction (verbatim below). DB-2: table format (columns: round, Player 1, Player 2, payoff). DB-3: system prompt →\to memory table →\to query; recent-first within table. DB-4: last H=5H{=}5 interactions, no retrieval beyond window. DB-5: hard window truncation at HH. DB-6: max_tokens 1024; no drop order needed (prompt ≪\ll budget). DB-7: name pool presented as list; order randomized per call. DR-1: case-insensitive regex CHOICE:\s*(\S+), quotes stripped, matched against the name pool; if that fails, the last line of the output that equals a pool name (exact code below). DR-2: output must be in name pool. DR-3: resample up to 3 times with identical prompt; uniform random on final failure. DR-4: uniform random choice; other agents observe a valid name (no null actions). DR-5: 0.4% (127/32,000 calls across all arms). DF-1: no third-party framework; custom implementation.

Verbatim prompts (baseline arm).

The system prompt is three blocks joined by blank lines; {pool} is the name pool in a per-call random order (DB-7), and the memory table holds the last H=5H{=}5 interactions, most recent first. With an empty memory, the table block is replaced by “Player 1 has no interaction history yet. This is their first interaction.”

[system]
You are observing a coordination game between two players. In each round,
both players simultaneously choose a name from the pool: {pool}. If both
players choose the same name, each earns +100 points. If they choose
different names, each loses 50 points. Player 1’s objective is to maximize
their own accumulated point tally, conditional on the behavior of their
co-player. You will predict what Player 1 will choose next based on their
history.

Player 1’s interaction history (most recent first):

| Round | Player 1’s Choice | Co-player’s Choice | Outcome | Payoff |
|-------|-------------|------------------|---------|--------|
| {round} | {own} | {partner} | {Match|Mismatch} | {+100|-50} |
...

Player 1’s accumulated score: {window_sum}

Think step by step, then predict Player 1’s next choice. Keep your
reasoning brief (2-3 sentences).

You MUST end your response with exactly this line:
CHOICE: <name>

where <name> is one of the names from the pool.

[user]
What name will Player 1 choose in the next interaction?

The first-person arm (M4) replaces the observer wording with second-person wording (“You are playing a coordination game with another player…”, “What name do you choose for this interaction?”); the other arms change only the memory block.

Parser and retry (DR-1 to DR-4).

def parse_choice(raw_output, name_pool):
    m = re.search(r"CHOICE:\s*(\S+)", raw_output, re.IGNORECASE)
    if m:
        cand = m.group(1).strip().strip(’"’).strip("’")
        for name in name_pool:
            if cand.upper() == name.upper():
                return name
    for line in reversed(raw_output.strip().split("\n")):
        for name in name_pool:
            if line.strip().upper() == name.upper():
                return name
    return None   # parse failure

# DR-3: on None, resample with the identical prompt up to 3 times;
# DR-4: after the final failure, choose uniformly at random from the pool.

Block C mapping (per-role: agent).

CR1: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6 (dated model ID, not a rotating alias). CR2: not available (Bedrock does not expose system fingerprints). CR3: AWS Bedrock us-east-1, accessed 2026-07-20 through 2026-08-10. CR4: temperature 0.7, top_k 40, max_tokens 1024; 20 seeds per arm (seed_offset 0–19). CR5: provider-managed (Bedrock); precision not user-configurable. CR6: not applicable (no fine-tuning or adaptation).
